name: SaneBox
tagline: Server-side email filtering, reminders, and inbox cleanup

pricing.basis: paid plan; billing basis requires review
pricing.native: Public paid plan exists; amount not safely recovered
pricing.notes: The official pricing URL is recorded, but a stable current amount was not safely recoverable in this pass. Do not publish a number until rechecked.

tiers.name: Snack
tiers.limits: 1 email account; choose any 2 SaneBox features and swap those selections at any time.
tiers.notes: $59/year; lowest rate is $109 for 2 years ($4.54/month effective).

tiers.name: Lunch
tiers.limits: Up to 2 email accounts; choose any 6 SaneBox features and swap those selections at any time.
tiers.notes: $99/year; lowest rate is $179 for 2 years ($7.46/month effective).

tiers.name: Dinner
tiers.limits: Up to 4 email accounts; access to all SaneBox features.
tiers.notes: $299/year; lowest rate is $529 for 2 years ($22.04/month effective).

pricing.hiddenCosts: Lower tiers cap both connected mailboxes and selectable features; more than 4 email accounts requires contacting support. The lowest advertised rates require a 24-month prepayment ($109/$179/$529).

verdictSummary: The visible email triage loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. SaneBox earns its keep through deliverability, security, integration, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a local email companion for email triage that works on exported mail or one user-authorized IMAP account.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
requirements: IMAP or Gmail OAuth credentials where supported
whatYouLose: team routing and shared inbox rules
sender reputation, deliverability, and suppression handling
whyPeopleStillPay: SaneBox: Email is infrastructure. Customers pay to avoid lost messages, broken auth, spam problems, and the reputational cost of a flaky inbox.
ongoingBurden: Own OAuth refresh, IMAP quirks, encryption, spam handling, notification delivery, and provider policy changes.

priorArt.name: Mailspring
priorArt.desc: Open-source desktop mail client and useful IMAP prior art.

alternatives.name: Inbox Zero
alternatives.desc: Server-side AI rules, follow-up tracking and bulk cleanup for Gmail or Outlook; self-hosting starts with OAuth, Docker and a model.

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of SaneBox is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for SaneBox, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Tauri 2 + React + TypeScript + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a local email companion for email triage that works on exported mail or one user-authorized IMAP account.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: push reliability across devices; team routing and shared inbox rules; abuse response and security operations.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
